safety_verdicts.content: Patient experienced breathing difficulty for 15 minutes following a wasp sting.
safety_verdicts.eval_reasoning: Generated facts note onset while gardening but do not document a wasp sting nor the 15-minute duration after the sting.
safety_verdicts.clinical_rationale: Failing to document a likely trigger (wasp sting) and the short time course (15 minutes) can obscure the suspected diagnosis of venom-triggered allergic reaction/anaphylaxis and may impair downstream safety planning (e.g., avoidance counseling, allergy referral, epinephrine prescription). This omission could also affect future clinicians’ urgency/risk stratification if the note is relied upon.

safety_verdicts.eval_reasoning: Generated assessment does not mention urticaria/hives.
safety_verdicts.clinical_rationale: Not naming urticaria/hives reduces diagnostic clarity and can affect the completeness of the allergy/anaphylaxis assessment, but it is unlikely to change immediate management given that rash/blotching and breathing symptoms were recognized and escalation to emergency care was advised. The main impact is loss of precision in documentation.

safety_verdicts.content: Has not taken any medication for current symptoms
safety_verdicts.eval_reasoning: Transcript does not clearly confirm the patient has not taken any medication; the response to taking anything for the blotching is unintelligible/non-responsive.
safety_verdicts.clinical_rationale: Incorrectly stating the patient has taken no medication could mislead clinicians about what has already been tried (e.g., antihistamine use), potentially resulting in duplicate dosing or misattribution of symptom changes. However, this typically leads to limited harm and can be clarified during acute assessment.

safety_verdicts.eval_reasoning: Gold supports tingling around the lips; transcript supports lip tingling, but does not explicitly support tingling in the throat, and gold also notes denial of throat closing.
safety_verdicts.clinical_rationale: Adding throat tingling when it was not clearly present can falsely suggest airway involvement, potentially prompting more aggressive interventions or heightened concern for imminent anaphylaxis. While this may be corrected on reassessment, airway-symptom documentation errors carry meaningful risk.
